A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same study, dataset, and core decoding and encoding framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Sections 4.2–4.3 report original optical-flow decoding results and brain-encoding correlations for three participants, with additional cortical maps in Appendix C.

after.justification: The original empirical study remains, with additional generative-model comparisons, video reconstructions, and encoder-control results in Appendices A.3–A.4.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 adds a modular extension that supplies a MindVideo-decoded initial frame to the existing motion predictor and DragNUWA, enabling full video decoding. The core DINOv2-conditioned flow predictor, quantization, loss, and ridge-regression encoding procedure remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation with an initial frame generated from fMRI, extending coverage beyond conditioning on the observed first frame. Table S1 also evaluates SSV2-pretrained VideoMAE. The fMRI evaluation still uses the same Dynamic Natural Vision videos and three participants.

E2.justification: The motion comparison replaces v1's DINOv2-only, no-brain decoder baseline with Stable Video Diffusion and adds MindVideo and the Ours + MindVideo variant. Appendix A.4 additionally evaluates SSV2-pretrained VideoMAE and ImageNet-pretrained Hiera variants. These substantially expand and revise the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: Figure 3 replaces average masked EPE and cosine similarity with EPE restricted to pixels whose ground-truth motion exceeds 1% of frame width. New generative-baseline protocols select the lowest-EPE output from 100 MindVideo or 10 SVD samples per video. Appendix A.4 adds matched-architecture pretraining controls; the original fMRI splits and preprocessing remain.

E4.justification: Appendix A.4 adds analyses of encoding performance versus parameter count and pretraining sample count, plus controls varying VideoMAE training distribution and comparing equally sized Hiera models trained on images versus videos. Appendix A.3 adds generated-frame case studies. Conversely, v1's matched decoder-without-brain ablation is no longer reported.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly identifies error bars as standard errors, reports Holm-Bonferroni correction for decoding comparisons, and specifies a one-sample t-test for encoding results. Appendix A.4 adds correlation significance tests. These refine statistical reporting without establishing additional training runs; neither version reports training seeds or repeated-training counts.

E6.justification: v1 reports participant EPEs of 1.72, 1.72, and 1.76 against 2.00 for its image-only decoder; v2 reports thresholded EPEs of 0.543, 0.572, and 0.634 against 1.192 for SVD. These replace results under different metrics and comparators, rather than establish a same-setting gain. New hybrid-decoding and control results include Hiera Base Plus correlations of 0.2629 on K-400 versus 0.2198 on IN-1K in Table S2. Main Section 4.3 encoding scores are retained.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation of fMRI inputs, optical-flow fields, quantization, and prediction in Section 3.1 is retained. Neither version adds theoretical propositions, proofs, or substantive derivations; the revised evaluation threshold is a protocol change.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add full video decoding from brain activity as a principal contribution and explicitly claim more accurate motion decoding than MindVideo. The original motion-decoding, animation, and encoding claims remain, while the contribution framing expands toward improving computer-vision systems using neural information.

C2.justification: Appendix A.4 introduces substantive arguments about architecture and training paradigm explaining encoding advantages, interpreting size and data-volume correlations as evidence about confounding. Appendix A.3 acknowledges that decoded initial frames can depict incorrect content and argues that preserved motion demonstrates control by the predicted flow. These expand the mechanism explanations; the existing generalization and cross-participant limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents RAFT-based flow extraction and candidate selection for the new video baselines, provides additional encoder pretraining and size information, and adds a website link for animation examples. Existing flow quantization, hardware, training-time, preprocessing, and dataset-access disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially beyond the earlier image-decoding discussion and MindVideo comparison. v2 positions naturalistic object-level motion decoding against dot-motion and single-neuron studies, adds video-reconstruction research such as NeuroClips, and develops a broader brain–computer-vision motivation. These are substantive positioning changes beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The title changes, and the abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around reanimation and computer-vision benefits. The introduction separates Immediate Contributions from Larger Objectives, terminology and captions are edited throughout, and the supplement is reorganized into numbered subsections with a contents list.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, replaces Figure 1 with a broad pipeline overview, and redesigns Figure 3 as a grouped thresholded-EPE chart. It adds Figure 6, supplementary examples, control plots, and two tables. Existing appendix cortical maps are retained, enlarged, and rearranged: v1 Figures 10–26 become v2 Figures S6–S22.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central comparative claims: v1 quantitatively tested only an image-only decoder, whereas v2 directly evaluates SVD and MindVideo, demonstrates reconstruction without the true first frame, and adds architecture/pretraining controls. These address important gaps in comparative validation and interpretation. Losing the matched no-brain ablation and cosine metric removes useful diagnostic evidence, and nonsignificant correlations do not rule out confounding, but the new direct comparisons and controlled tests provide a substantial net improvement.
